newsitem.title: MONTSERRAT: Duke of York visits volcano-troubled Montserrat.
newsitem.headline: Duke of York visits volcano-troubled Montserrat.

text.p: Prince Andrew, the Duke of York, arrived on Tuesday for a tour of this British Caribbean colony, beset by a spewing volcano for nearly 19 months.
Officials hoped the prince's visit would boost their campaign for British aid to develop new housing in the island's north end, away from the rumbling mountain.
"We're always looking for advocates for our cause in the U.K.," said Montserrat Governor Frank Savage.
The prince was greeted by local dignitaries and a steel-drum band as he arrived at Montserrat's small seaside airport from neighbouring Antigua on a chartered nine-seat propeller plane.

His itinerary for the two-day visit included a tour of the island's ash-coated and largely abandoned capital, Plymouth, and visits to schools and public shelters at the north end, considered the safe zone.
The British Navy frigate HMS Boxer, on official duty in the West Indies, was stationed off Montserrat on Tuesday for the prince's visit, officials said.

The volcano in the Soufriere Hills roared to life in July 1995 following a century of virtual dormancy. Several dramatic eruptions since sent up towering ash clouds and belched rivers of hot rocks and gases that reached the sea.

Savage, the Queen's representative in the colony, said the prince was on a "working" visit to see first-hand the plight of the islanders, who were evacuated from the south end and the capital three times, the most recent 10 months ago.
"I want Montserratians to captivate him, capture his heart," Savage said.
Savage said the royal family took a keen interest in the disaster, which brought the local economy to a virtual standstill. Britain in August 1996 announced a $39 million development aid package.
Montserrat, a British dependent territory in the eastern Caribbean, is about 11 miles by 7 miles (17.6 km by 11.2 km) and lies about 27 miles (43 km) southwest of Antigua.
Its population, about 11,000 before the volcanic activity began, dropped to about 7,000 as residents left to find work in Britain or on neighbouring islands.
